questions.question: What is an Azure region?

options.text: A geographical area containing at least one, and potentially multiple, datacenters connected by a low-latency network
options.why: Correct.

options.text: A single server rack in a datacenter
options.why: A region contains whole datacenters, not a rack.

options.text: A logical container for resources
options.why: That is a resource group.

options.text: A billing account
options.why: Billing is handled by subscriptions and billing accounts.

questions.explanation: Regions are geographic areas with one or more datacenters networked together with low latency.

questions.question: Which TWO statements about Azure region pairs are true?

options.text: Planned Azure updates are rolled out to paired regions one region at a time
options.why: Correct. This reduces the risk of both being affected.

options.text: Every region pair is always in different continents
options.why: Pairs are usually in the same geography.

options.text: If a broad outage occurs, recovery of one region in each pair is prioritised
options.why: Correct.

options.text: Resources are automatically replicated to the paired region for every service
options.why: Replication depends on the service and your configuration (for example GRS).

questions.explanation: Region pairs provide sequential updates and prioritised recovery; replication is service-specific.

questions.question: Azure Government is an example of which type of region?

options.text: Sovereign region
options.why: Correct. It is isolated for US government agencies and partners.

options.text: Availability zone
options.why: Zones are within a region.

options.text: Region pair
options.why: A pair is two regions linked for resilience.

options.text: Edge zone only
options.why: Azure Government is a sovereign cloud.

questions.explanation: Sovereign regions such as Azure Government (US) and Azure operated by 21Vianet (China) are isolated from the main Azure cloud.

questions.question: What is an availability zone?

options.text: A physically separate location within an Azure region, made up of one or more datacenters with independent power, cooling and networking
options.why: Correct.

options.text: A group of regions in the same country
options.why: That is a geography.

options.text: A logical grouping of VMs inside one rack
options.why: That is closer to a fault domain in an availability set.

options.text: A type of subscription
options.why: Zones are physical infrastructure.

questions.explanation: Availability zones are isolated datacenter groups within a region. Zone-enabled regions have at least three.

questions.question: A service that automatically replicates across availability zones, so you do not choose a specific zone, is described as what?

options.text: Zone-redundant
options.why: Correct.

options.text: Zonal
options.why: Zonal services are pinned to a specific zone you choose.

options.text: Non-regional
options.why: Non-regional services are global and not tied to a region.

options.text: Sovereign
options.why: Sovereign refers to isolated clouds.

questions.explanation: Zonal = pinned to one zone; zone-redundant = replicated across zones automatically; non-regional = always available globally.

questions.question: Which statement about resource groups is true?

options.text: A resource can belong to only one resource group at a time
options.why: Correct.

options.text: Resource groups can be nested inside other resource groups
options.why: Resource groups cannot be nested.

options.text: All resources in a resource group must be in the same region
options.why: Resources can be in different regions from each other and from the group.

options.text: Deleting a resource group leaves its resources running
options.why: Deleting a resource group deletes everything inside it.

questions.explanation: Each resource lives in exactly one resource group; groups cannot be nested; deleting a group deletes its contents.

questions.scenario: A developer creates a temporary test environment containing a VM, a database and a storage account. When testing ends, everything must be removed quickly.
questions.question: What is the simplest approach?

options.text: Put all the resources in one resource group and delete the group afterwards
options.why: Correct. Deleting the group deletes all its resources.

options.text: Put each resource in a different subscription
options.why: This adds complexity with no benefit.

options.text: Apply a ReadOnly lock
options.why: A lock would prevent changes and deletion.

options.text: Create a management group
options.why: Management groups organise subscriptions, not resources for cleanup.

questions.explanation: Grouping resources with the same lifecycle in one resource group makes cleanup a single action.

questions.question: An Azure subscription acts as which TWO types of boundary?

options.text: Billing boundary
options.why: Correct. Each subscription gets its own invoices and cost reports.

options.text: Physical datacenter boundary
options.why: Subscriptions are logical, not physical.

options.text: Access control boundary
options.why: Correct. Access policies can be applied per subscription.

options.text: Availability zone boundary
options.why: Zones are physical infrastructure in a region.

questions.explanation: Subscriptions are both billing and access-control boundaries.

questions.scenario: A company has 40 subscriptions and wants to apply the same Azure Policy and access rules to all subscriptions belonging to its Finance division.
questions.question: What should it use?

options.text: A management group containing the Finance subscriptions
options.why: Correct. Policies and RBAC applied to a management group are inherited.

options.text: A single resource group
options.why: Resource groups live inside one subscription.

options.text: A resource tag
options.why: Tags add metadata but do not apply policy inheritance.

options.text: A virtual network
options.why: Networking is unrelated.

questions.explanation: Management groups organise subscriptions so governance can be applied once and inherited.

questions.question: Which order shows the Azure management hierarchy from the HIGHEST level to the LOWEST?

options.text: Management groups → subscriptions → resource groups → resources
options.why: Correct.

options.text: Subscriptions → management groups → resources → resource groups
options.why: Incorrect order.

options.text: Resource groups → subscriptions → management groups → resources
options.why: Incorrect order.

options.text: Resources → resource groups → subscriptions → management groups
options.why: This is lowest to highest.

questions.explanation: Management groups contain subscriptions, which contain resource groups, which contain resources.

questions.question: Azure Policy assigned at a management group applies to which resources?

options.text: All subscriptions, resource groups and resources beneath that management group
options.why: Correct. Settings are inherited down the hierarchy.

options.text: Only resources created directly in the management group
options.why: Resources are not created directly in management groups.

options.text: Only the first subscription under it
options.why: All child scopes inherit.

options.text: Only resources in the same region as the management group
options.why: Management groups are not regional.

questions.explanation: Policy and RBAC assignments inherit down from management groups to everything below.

questions.question: What does an Azure datacenter provide?

options.text: The physical facilities, with servers, power, cooling and networking, that host Azure resources
options.why: Correct.

options.text: A logical folder for organising resources
options.why: That is a resource group.

options.text: A list of compliance policies
options.why: That is Azure Policy or Purview.

options.text: A software development kit
options.why: SDKs are libraries, not facilities.

questions.explanation: Datacenters are the physical buildings, grouped into availability zones and regions. Customers cannot choose an individual datacenter directly.
